# std_logger - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/std-logger/*/std_logger/

## Expand description

A crate that holds a logging implementation that logs to standard error and
standard out. It uses standard error for all regular messages and standard
out for requests. To initialise the logger use [ Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html).

This crate provides only a logging implementation. To do actual logging use
the [ log](https://crates.io/crates/log) crate and it’s various macros.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-formats)Supported Formats

This crate supports the three following formats:

- Logfmt, following [https://www.brandur.org/logfmt](https://www.brandur.org/logfmt), use`Config::logfmt`
- JSON, use `Config::json`
- Google Cloud Platform structured logging using JSON, following
[https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/structured-logging](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/structured-logging),`Config::gcloud`

[§](https://docs.rs#logfmt)Logfmt

For regular messages, printed to standard error, Logfmt looks like the following:

```
ts="YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.MICROSZ" lvl="$LOG_LEVEL" msg="$message" target="$target" module="$module"
For example:
ts="2018-03-24T13:48:28.820588Z" lvl="ERROR" msg="my error message" target="my_module" module="my_module"
```
Requests or access messages, logged using the [ REQUEST_TARGET](https://docs.rs/constant.REQUEST_TARGET.html) target or
the

[macro, are printed to standard out using following format:](https://docs.rs/macro.request.html)

`request````
ts="YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.MICROSZ" lvl="INFO" msg="$message" target="request" module="$module"
For example:
ts="2018-03-24T13:30:28.820588Z" lvl="INFO" msg="my request message" target="request" module="my_module"
```
Note: the timestamp is not printed when the *timestamp* feature is not
enabled, this feature is enabled by default, see [Timestamp feature](https://docs.rs#timestamp-feature) below.

[§](https://docs.rs#json-ndjson)JSON (NDJSON)

Formatting using JSON uses one object per limit, which looks like the following:

```
{"timestamp":"YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.MICROSZ","level":"$LOG_LEVEL","message":"$message","target":"$module","module":"$module"}
For example:
{"timestamp":"2018-03-24T13:48:28.820588Z","level":"ERROR","message":"my error message","target":"my_module","module":"my_module"}
```
Note: the timestamp is not printed when the *timestamp* feature is not
enabled, this feature is enabled by default, see [Timestamp feature](https://docs.rs#timestamp-feature) below.

[§](https://docs.rs#gcloud-gcp-json)Gcloud (GCP JSON)

Google Cloud Platform structured logging using JSON, or just gcloud for short, uses JSON for messages. Regular messages are printed to standard error and look like the following:

```
{"timestamp":"YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.MICROSZ","severity":"$LOG_LEVEL","message":"$message","target":"$module","module":"$module"}
For example:
{"timestamp":"2018-03-24T13:48:28.820588Z","severity":"ERROR","message":"my error message","target":"my_module","module":"my_module"}
```
Note: the timestamp is not printed when the *timestamp* feature is not
enabled, this feature is enabled by default, see [Timestamp feature](https://docs.rs#timestamp-feature) below.

The format for requests looks the same, but are logged to standard out. There are some things to note that are special for the gcloud format:

- Panics are logged using the `CRITICAL`severity instead of`ERROR`.
- When debug logging is enabled `sourceLocation`is added with the file and line information to all logs, if the source information is provided.

[§](https://docs.rs#setting-severity)Setting severity

You can use various environment variables to change the severity (log level) of the messages to actually log and which to ignore.

`LOG` and `LOG_LEVEL` can be used to set the severity to a specific value,
see the [ log](https://crates.io/crates/log)’s package

[type for available values.](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.29/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`LevelFilter````
## In your shell of your choice:
## Set the log severity to only print log messages with info severity or
## higher, trace and debug messages won't be printed anymore.
$ LOG=info ./my_binary
## Set the log severity to only print log messages with warning severity or
## higher, informational (or lower severity) messages won't be printed
## anymore.
$ LOG=warn ./my_binary
```
Alternatively setting the `TRACE` variable (e.g. `TRACE=1`) sets the
severity to the trace, meaning it will log everything. Setting `DEBUG` will
set the severity to debug.

```
## In your shell of your choice:
## Enables trace logging.
$ TRACE=1 ./my_binary
## Enables debug logging.
$ DEBUG=1 ./my_binary
```
If none of these environment variables are found it will default to an information severity.

In addition to these runtime filters the [log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.29/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/index.html) crate provides [compile time
filters](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.29/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/index.html#compile-time-filters) which allows you to filter log messages at compile time.

[§](https://docs.rs#logging-requests)Logging requests

To log requests a special target is provided: [ REQUEST_TARGET](https://docs.rs/constant.REQUEST_TARGET.html) and a
special macro:

[. This will cause the message to be logged to standard out, rather then standard error. This allows for separate processing of error messages and request logs.](https://docs.rs/macro.request.html)

`request````
use std_logger::request;
request!("Got a request!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limiting-logging-targets)Limiting logging targets

Sometimes it’s useful to only log messages related to a specific target, for
example when debugging a single function you might want only see messages
from the module the function is in. This can be achieved by using the
`LOG_TARGET` environment variable.

```
## In your shell of choose:
## Only log messages from your crate.
$ LOG_TARGET=my_crate ./my_binary
## Only log messages from the `my_module` module in your crate.
$ LOG_TARGET=my_crate::my_module ./my_binary
## Multiple log targets are also supported by separating the values by a comma.
$ LOG_TARGET=my_crate::my_module,my_crate::my_other_module ./my_binary
## Very useful in combination with trace severity to get all messages you
## want, but filter out the messages for crates you're not interested in.
$ LOG_LEVEL=trace LOG_TARGET=my_crate::my_module ./my_binary
```
Note that [requests](https://docs.rs/index.html#logging-requests) and panics (with [target=“panic”](https://docs.rs/constant.PANIC_TARGET.html)) are always logged.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

This crate has three features:

- *timestamp*, enabled by default.
- *log-panic*, enabled by default.
- *nightly*, disabled by default.
- *serde1*, disabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#timestamp-feature)Timestamp feature

The *timestamp* feature adds a timestamp in front of every message. It uses
the format defined in [ RFC3339](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3339) with 6 digit microsecond precision, e.g.

`2018-03-24T13:48:48.063934Z`. The timestamp is **always**logged in UTC.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

This feature uses [ SystemTime](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/time/struct.SystemTime.html) as time source, which

**is not monotonic**. This means that a log message created after an

*earlier*log message can have a timestamp

**before**the earlier created log message.

[§](https://docs.rs#log-panic-feature)Log-panic feature

The *log-panic* feature will log all panics using the `error` severity,
rather then using the default panic handler. It will log the panic message
as well as the location and a backtrace, see the log output below for an
example (this example doesn’t include a timestamp).

```
lvl="ERROR" msg="thread 'main' panicked at 'oops', examples/panic.rs:24" target="panic" module="" backtrace="
stack backtrace:
   0:        0x106ba8f74 - backtrace::backtrace::trace<closure>
                        at backtrace-0.3.2/src/backtrace/mod.rs:42
   1:        0x106ba49af - backtrace::capture::Backtrace::new::h54d7cfa8f40c5b43
                        at backtrace-0.3.2/src/capture.rs:64
   2:        0x106b9f4e6 - log_panics::init::{{closure}}
                        at log-panics-1.2.0/src/lib.rs:52
   3:        0x106bc6951 - std::panicking::rust_panic_with_hook::h6c19f9ba35264287
                        at src/libstd/panicking.rs:612
   4:        0x106b93146 - std::panicking::begin_panic<&str>
                        at src/libstd/panicking.rs:572
   5:        0x106b93bf1 - panic::main
                        at examples/panic.rs:24
   6:        0x106bc751c - __rust_maybe_catch_panic
                        at src/libpanic_unwind/lib.rs:98
   7:        0x106bc6c08 - std::rt::lang_start::h6f338c4ae2d58bbe
                        at src/libstd/rt.rs:61
   8:        0x106b93c29 - main
"
```
If the *timestamp* feature is enable the first line of the message will be
prefixed with a timestamp as described in the [Timestamp feature](https://docs.rs#timestamp-feature).

[§](https://docs.rs#nightly-feature)Nightly feature

Enabling this feature enables the crate to use unstable (i.e. nightly-only) features from the compiler and standard library.

Currently this enables nothing.

[§](https://docs.rs#serde1-feature)Serde1 feature

Enables the use of [serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde) version 1. Mainly this allows the value of
key-value pairs to be structured.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::info;
use std_logger::request;
fn main() {
    // First thing we need to do is initialise the logger before anything
    // else.
    std_logger::Config::logfmt().init();
    // Now we can start logging!
    info!("Our application started!");
    // Do useful stuff, like starting a HTTP server.
}
/// This our example request handler, just pretend it gets called with a
/// request.
fn log_handler(req: Request) {
    // This will be logged to standard out, rather then standard error.
    request!(
        url = req.url,
        status = req.status,
        response_time:? = req.response_time;
        "HTTP request"
    );
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [request](https://docs.rs/macro.request.html)
- Logs a request.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html)
- Configuration of the logger.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [PANIC_](https://docs.rs/constant.PANIC_TARGET.html)- TARGET
- Target for logging panics.
- [REQUEST_](https://docs.rs/constant.REQUEST_TARGET.html)- TARGET
- Target for logging requests.

# structured_logger - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/structured-logger/latest/structured_logger/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#structured-logger)Structured Logger

A logging implementation for the [ log](https://crates.io/crates/log) crate that logs structured values
either synchronous or asynchronous, in JSON, CBOR, or any other format,
to a file, stderr, stdout, or any other destination.
To initialize the logger use the

[struct. It is inspired by](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html)

`Builder`[std-logger](https://github.com/Thomasdezeeuw/std-logger).

This crate provides only a logging implementation. To do actual logging use
the [ log](https://crates.io/crates/log) crate and it’s various macros.

[§](https://docs.rs#limiting-logging-targets)Limiting logging targets

You can use [ Builder::with_target_writer](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.with_target_writer) method to log messages related specific target to a specific writer.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

This crate has three features:

- `log-panic`, enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#log-panic-feature)Log-panic feature

The `log-panic` feature will log all panics using the `error` severity,
rather then using the default panic handler. It will log the panic message
as well as the location and a backtrace, see the log output for an
[ panic_log](https://github.com/iorust/structured-logger/blob/main/examples/panic_log.rs) example.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

- Log panics example: [https://github.com/iorust/structured-logger/blob/main/examples/panic_log.rs](https://github.com/iorust/structured-logger/blob/main/examples/panic_log.rs)
- Async log example: [https://github.com/iorust/structured-logger/blob/main/examples/async_log.rs](https://github.com/iorust/structured-logger/blob/main/examples/async_log.rs)

Simple example:

```
use serde::Serialize;
use structured_logger::{async_json::new_writer, unix_ms, Builder};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // Initialize the logger.
    Builder::with_level("info")
        .with_target_writer("*", new_writer(tokio::io::stdout()))
        .init();
    // Or use the default:
    // structured_logger::init();
    let kv = ContextLog {
        uid: "user123".to_string(),
        action: "upate_book".to_string(),
    };
    log::info!("hello world");
    // This log will be written to stdout:
    // {"level":"INFO","message":"hello world","target":"simple","timestamp":1679745592127}
    log::info!(target: "api",
        method = "GET",
        path = "/hello",
        status = 200_u16,
        start = unix_ms(),
        elapsed = 10_u64,
        kv:serde = kv;
        "",
    );
    // This log will be written to stdout:
    // {"elapsed":10,"kv":{"uid":"user123","action":"upate_book"},"level":"INFO","message":"","method":"GET","path":"/hello","start":1679745592127,"status":200,"target":"api","timestamp":1679745592127}
}
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ContextLog {
    uid: String,
    action: String,
}
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [async_](https://docs.rs/async_json/index.html)- json
- Async JSON Writer Implementation
- [json](https://docs.rs/json/index.html)
- Sync JSON Writer Implementation

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Writer](https://docs.rs/trait.Writer.html)
- A trait that defines how to write a log. You can implement this trait for your custom formatting and writing destination.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_env_level.html)- env_ - level
- Returns the log level from the environment variables: `LOG`,`LOG_LEVEL`,`RUST_LOG`,`TRACE`or`DEBUG`. Default is`INFO`.
- [init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html)
- Initializes the logger for `log`
- [log_](https://docs.rs/fn.log_failure.html)- failure
- A fallback logging function that is used in case of logging failure in `Writer``stderr`.
- [unix_ms](https://docs.rs/fn.unix_ms.html)
- Returns the current unix timestamp in milliseconds.

# clang_log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clang_log/latest/clang_log

## Expand description

I really like the logging format of `clang` (pronounced klang, not C-lang), so I recreated it as an implementation of the `log` crate. It’s licensed under the MIT license, and you can use it as you like. Use it, fork it, steal the code and sell it, I don’t really care. If you find bugs, first of all, good job, because how can a logging implementation have bugs, and second of all, you can submit them to the issue tracker, or fix them and submit a PR. Additionally, if you want to improve `clang_log`, go ahead and waste five minuites writing a PR to change something.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use)How to use

To use `clang_log`, first include it, and `log` in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
log = "0.4.27"
clang_log = "2.1.2"
```
`clang_log` also has a feature flag; `color`. By removing this feature flag, you can remove color from the output.

```
[dependencies]
log = "0.4.27"
clang_log = { version = "2.1.2", default-features = false }
```
After adding `clang_log` to `Cargo.toml`, initialize it at the start of the program:

```
use log::Level;
fn main() {
    clang_log::init(Level::Trace, "clang")
}
```
You can also specify a minimum level to start outputting to stderr:

```
use log::Level;
fn main() {
    clang_log::init_error(Level::Trace, Level::Warn, "clang")
}
```
To use it, just use the macros provided by `log`

```
use log::*;
error!("Could not find files!");
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Logger](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html)
- Logger struct. Use `init()`instead, since`Logger`is useless without it being set as the logger, and`init()`does that anyway.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html)
- Initialize logger with fields
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_error.html)- error
- Initialize logger with fields.

# ftail - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ftail/latest/ftail

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#ftail)Ftail

**Ftail** is a simple logging implementation for the [ log](https://crates.io/crates/log) crate with support for multiple channels, including console output, files, and custom loggers.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Multiple logging channels: console, formatted console, single file, daily file, and custom
- Level and target filtering
- Optional timestamp formatting and timezone support
- Automatic log rotation and retention
- Use `RUST_LOG`environment variable for dynamic log level control (use ‘_env_level’ postfix)

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

Add Ftail to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
ftail = "0.3"
```
Initialize Ftail in your `main.rs` or `lib.rs`:

```
use ftail::Ftail;
use log::LevelFilter;
fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    Ftail::new()
        .console(LevelFilter::Info)        // log to console
        .daily_file("logs", LevelFilter::Error) // log errors to daily files
        .init()?; // initialize logger
    log::info!("Hello, Ftail!");
    log::error!("This is an error message");
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#configuration-options)Configuration Options

| Option | Description | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `.datetime_format()` | Set the datetime format | Ex: `"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%.3f"` |
| `.timezone()` | Set the timezone | Requires `timezone`feature |
| `.max_file_size()` | Maximum file size in MB | Older logs renamed `.old{N}` |
| `.retention_days()` | Number of days to keep log files | Daily file only |
| `.filter_levels()` | Log only the specified levels | `Vec<Level>` |
| `.filter_targets()` | Log only the specified targets | `Vec<&str>` |

[§](https://docs.rs#channels)Channels

[§](https://docs.rs#console)Console

Logs to the standard output without formatting.

```
Ftail::new()
    .console(LevelFilter::Trace)
    .init()?;
```
**Output:**

```
2024-09-13 17:35:18 TRACE console This is a trace message
2024-09-13 17:35:18 DEBUG console This is a debug message
2024-09-13 17:35:18 INFO foo bar
2024-09-13 17:35:18 WARN console This is a warning message
2024-09-13 17:35:18 ERROR console This is an error message
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatted-console)Formatted Console

Logs with formatted and colored output.

```
Ftail::new()
    .formatted_console(LevelFilter::Trace)
    .init()?;
```
**Output:**

```
2024-09-13 17:35:37 · TRACE
This is a trace message
examples/formatted_console/src/main.rs:9
2024-09-13 17:35:37 · DEBUG
This is a debug message
examples/formatted_console/src/main.rs:11
```
[§](https://docs.rs#single-file)Single File

Logs to a single file (e.g., `logs/demo.log`).

```
Ftail::new()
    .single_file(Path::new("logs/demo.log"), true, LevelFilter::Trace)
    .init()?;
```
- `append = true`keeps existing logs,- `false`overwrites.

[§](https://docs.rs#daily-file)Daily File

Logs to daily files in a directory (e.g., `logs/2025-09-25.log`).

```
Ftail::new()
    .daily_file(Path::new("logs"), LevelFilter::Trace)
    .init()?;
```
- Automatically rotates files per day.

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-channel)Custom Channel

Create your own logger by implementing the `log::Log` trait:

```
Ftail::new()
    .custom(
        |config| Box::new(CustomLogger { config }) as Box<dyn Log + Send + Sync>,
        LevelFilter::Debug,
    )
    .datetime_format("%H:%M:%S%.3f")
    .init()?;
struct CustomLogger {
    config: ftail::Config,
}
impl log::Log for CustomLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &log::Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= self.config.level_filter
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &log::Record) {
        if !self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            return;
        }
        let time = chrono::Local::now()
            .format(&self.config.datetime_format)
            .to_string();
        println!("[{}] {}: {}", time, record.level(), record.args());
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
```
**Output:**

```
19:37:22.402 [DEBUG] This is a debug message
19:37:22.403 [INFO] bar
19:37:22.403 [WARN] This is a warning message
19:37:22.403 [ERROR] This is an error message
```
[§](https://docs.rs#tips)Tips

- Use `.console(LevelFilter::Debug)`for development.
- Use `.daily_file()`in production to organize logs by date.
- Combine `.max_file_size()`and`.retention_days()`to prevent disk bloat.
- Only enable the channels you need to reduce overhead by disabling default features in `Cargo.toml`.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ansi_](https://docs.rs/ansi_escape/index.html)- escape
- Module containing the ANSI escape codes.
- [channels](https://docs.rs/channels/index.html)
- Module containing the channels.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Module containing the error type.

---

# log4rs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log4rs/*/log4rs/

## Expand description

log4rs is a highly configurable logging framework modeled after Java’s Logback and log4j libraries.

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

The basic units of configuration are *appenders*, *encoders*, *filters*, and
*loggers*.

[§](https://docs.rs#appenders)Appenders

An appender takes a log record and logs it somewhere, for example, to a file, the console, or the syslog.

Implementations:

- [console](https://docs.rs/append/console/struct.ConsoleAppenderDeserializer.html#configuration): requires the- `console_appender`feature.
- [file](https://docs.rs/append/file/struct.FileAppenderDeserializer.html#configuration): requires the- `file_appender`feature.
- [rolling_file](https://docs.rs/append/rolling_file/struct.RollingFileAppenderDeserializer.html#configuration): requires the- `rolling_file_appender`feature and can be configured with the- `compound_policy`.

[§](https://docs.rs#encoders)Encoders

An encoder is responsible for taking a log record, transforming it into the appropriate output format, and writing it out. An appender will normally use an encoder internally.

Implementations:

[§](https://docs.rs#filters)Filters

Filters are associated with appenders and, like the name would suggest, filter log events coming into that appender.

Implementations:

- [threshold](https://docs.rs/filter/threshold/struct.ThresholdFilterDeserializer.html#configuration): requires the- `threshold_filter`feature

[§](https://docs.rs#loggers)Loggers

A log event is targeted at a specific logger, which are identified by
string names. The logging macros built in to the `log` crate set the logger
of a log event to the one identified by the module containing the
invocation location.

Loggers form a hierarchy: logger names are divided into components by “::”. One logger is the ancestor of another if the first logger’s component list is a prefix of the second logger’s component list.

Loggers are associated with a maximum log level. Log events for that logger with a level above the maximum will be ignored. The maximum log level for any logger can be configured manually; if it is not, the level will be inherited from the logger’s parent.

Loggers are also associated with a set of appenders. Appenders can be
associated directly with a logger. In addition, the appenders of the
logger’s parent will be associated with the logger unless the logger has
its *additive* set to `false`. Log events sent to the logger that are not
filtered out by the logger’s maximum log level will be sent to all
associated appenders.

The “root” logger is the ancestor of all other loggers. Since it has no ancestors, its additivity cannot be configured.

[§](https://docs.rs#configuration)Configuration

For a detailed breakdown on configuration, refer to the
[config module](https://docs.rs/config/index.html#configuration).

log4rs makes heavy use of Cargo features to enable consumers to pick the
functionality they wish to use. File-based configuration requires the `file`
feature, and each file format requires its own feature as well. In addition,
each component has its own feature. For example, YAML support requires the
`yaml_format` feature and the console appender requires the
`console_appender` feature.

By default, the `all_components`, `gzip`, `file`, and `yaml_format` features
are enabled.

As a convenience, the `all_components` feature activates all logger components.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#configuration-via-a-yaml-file)Configuration via a YAML file

```
# Scan this file for changes every 30 seconds
refresh_rate: 30 seconds
appenders:
  # An appender named "stdout" that writes to stdout
  stdout:
    kind: console
  # An appender named "requests" that writes to a file with a custom pattern encoder
  requests:
    kind: file
    path: "log/requests.log"
    encoder:
      pattern: "{d} - {m}{n}"
# Set the default logging level to "warn" and attach the "stdout" appender to the root
root:
  level: warn
  appenders:
    - stdout
loggers:
  # Raise the maximum log level for events sent to the "app::backend::db" logger to "info"
  app::backend::db:
    level: info
  # Route log events sent to the "app::requests" logger to the "requests" appender,
  # and *not* the normal appenders installed at the root
  app::requests:
    level: info
    appenders:
      - requests
    additive: false
```
Add the following in your application initialization.

`log4rs::init_file("log4rs.yml", Default::default()).unwrap();`[§](https://docs.rs#programmatically-constructing-a-configuration)Programmatically constructing a configuration:

```
use log::LevelFilter;
use log4rs::append::console::ConsoleAppender;
use log4rs::append::file::FileAppender;
use log4rs::encode::pattern::PatternEncoder;
use log4rs::config::{Appender, Config, Logger, Root};
fn main() {
    let stdout = ConsoleAppender::builder().build();
    let requests = FileAppender::builder()
        .encoder(Box::new(PatternEncoder::new("{d} - {m}{n}")))
        .build("log/requests.log")
        .unwrap();
    let config = Config::builder()
        .appender(Appender::builder().build("stdout", Box::new(stdout)))
        .appender(Appender::builder().build("requests", Box::new(requests)))
        .logger(Logger::builder().build("app::backend::db", LevelFilter::Info))
        .logger(Logger::builder()
            .appender("requests")
            .additive(false)
            .build("app::requests", LevelFilter::Info))
        .build(Root::builder().appender("stdout").build(LevelFilter::Warn))
        .unwrap();
    let handle = log4rs::init_config(config).unwrap();
    // use handle to change logger configuration at runtime
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-implementations-of-logging-components)Custom implementations of logging components

You can impl some trait for your struct and use it with log4rs. For example:

- Impl [log4rs::append::Append](https://docs.rs/append/trait.Append.html)for your custom appender.
- Impl [log4rs::encode::Encode](https://docs.rs/encode/trait.Encode.html)for your custom encoder.
- Impl [log4rs::filter::Filter](https://docs.rs/filter/trait.Filter.html)for your custom filter.

Here is a very simple example to create a custom appender,
for more examples about custom, see [examples/custom.rs](https://github.com/estk/log4rs/tree/main/examples/custom.rs):

```
use log4rs::append::Append;
use log4rs::config::{Appender, Root};
#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyAppender(usize);
// impl your process record logic here
impl Append for MyAppender {
    fn append(&self, record: &log::Record) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        println!("appender({}): {record:?}", self.0);
        Ok(())
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
fn main() {
    let appender = MyAppender(100);
    let log_config = log4rs::config::Config::builder()
        .appender(Appender::builder().build("my_appender", Box::new(appender)))
        .build(
            Root::builder()
                .appender("my_appender")
                .build(log::LevelFilter::Info),
        )
        .unwrap();
    log4rs::init_config(log_config).unwrap();
    log::trace!("This is a trace message");
    log::info!("This is an info message");
    log::warn!("This is a warning message");
}
```
To configure log4rs with a file, you should implement [log4rs::config::Deserialize](https://docs.rs/config/trait.Deserialize.html) for your config and be sure to register it with [log4rs::config::Deserializers](https://docs.rs/config/struct.Deserializers.html) as shown in the example below.

Here is a very simple example to use a custom appender with custom config.
For more examples about custom config file, see [examples/custom_config.rs](https://github.com/estk/log4rs/tree/main/examples/custom_config.rs):

```
# custom_config.yml
appenders:
  my_appender:
    kind: custom_appender
    appender_data: 42
root:
  level: INFO
  appenders:
    - my_appender
```
```
use log4rs::append::Append;
use log4rs::config::{Deserialize, Deserializers};
#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyAppender(usize);
// impl your process record logic here
impl Append for MyAppender {
    fn append(&self, record: &log::Record) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        println!("appender({}): {record:?}", self.0);
        Ok(())
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
// Define config struct for custom appender
#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
pub struct MyAppenderConfig {
    pub appender_data: Option<usize>,
}
#[derive(Default)]
pub struct MyAppenderDeserializer;
// impl Deserialize for custom appender config
impl Deserialize for MyAppenderDeserializer {
    type Trait = dyn Append;
    type Config = MyAppenderConfig;
    fn deserialize(
        &self,
        config: MyAppenderConfig,
        _: &Deserializers,
    ) -> anyhow::Result<Box<Self::Trait>> {
        let appender_data = config.appender_data.unwrap_or(0);
        let appender = MyAppender(appender_data);
        Ok(Box::new(appender))
    }
}
fn main() {
    let log_file = "custom_config.yml";
    // Access the default deserializers map
    let mut deserializers = Deserializers::default();
    // Register the "custom_appender" deserializer into the default deserializers map
    deserializers.insert("custom_appender", MyAppenderDeserializer);
    // Initialize log4rs with the custom deserializers from the file
    log4rs::init_file(log_file, deserializers).unwrap();
    log::trace!("This is a trace message");
    log::info!("This is an info message");
    log::warn!("This is a warning message");
}
```
For more examples see the [examples](https://github.com/estk/log4rs/tree/main/examples).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use config::`- [init_config](https://docs.rs/config/fn.init_config.html);
- `pub use config::`- [Config](https://docs.rs/config/runtime/struct.Config.html);
- `pub use config::`- [init_file](https://docs.rs/config/fn.init_file.html);
- `pub use config::`- [init_raw_config](https://docs.rs/config/fn.init_raw_config.html);

# logforth - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/logforth/*/logforth/

## Expand description

Logforth is a flexible logging framework for Rust applications, providing easy log dispatching and configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

Logforth allows you to set up multiple log dispatches with different filters and appenders. You can configure global log levels, use built-in appenders for stdout, stderr, files, or create custom appenders.

It provides out-of-the-box integrations with the `log` crate:

```
cargo add log
cargo add logforth -F starter-log
```
[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Simple setup with a stderr appender:

```
logforth::starter_log::stderr().apply();
log::info!("This is an info message.");
```
Advanced setup with custom filters and multiple appenders:

```
use logforth::append;
use logforth::record::Level;
use logforth::record::LevelFilter;
logforth::starter_log::builder()
    .dispatch(|d| {
        d.filter(LevelFilter::MoreSevereEqual(Level::Error))
            .append(append::Stderr::default())
    })
    .dispatch(|d| {
        d.filter(LevelFilter::MoreSevereEqual(Level::Info))
            .append(append::Stdout::default())
    })
    .apply();
log::error!("Error message.");
log::info!("Info message.");
```
See the [README](https://github.com/fast/logforth?tab=readme-ov-file) file for more details and examples.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [append](https://docs.rs/append/index.html)
- Dispatch log records to various targets.
- [bridge](https://docs.rs/bridge/index.html)
- Bridge logforth with other logging frameworks.
- [core](https://docs.rs/core/index.html)
- Core components of the logforth logging framework.
- [diagnostic](https://docs.rs/diagnostic/index.html)
- Mapped Diagnostic Context (MDC).
- [filter](https://docs.rs/filter/index.html)
- Filters for log records.
- [kv](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html)
- Key-value pairs in a log record or a diagnostic context.
- [layout](https://docs.rs/layout/index.html)
- Layouts for formatting log records.
- [record](https://docs.rs/record/index.html)
- Log record and metadata.
- [starter_](https://docs.rs/starter_log/index.html)- log - `starter-log`
- Starter configurations for quickly setting up logforth with the `log`crate
- [trap](https://docs.rs/trap/index.html)
- Traps for processing errors.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- The error struct of logforth.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Append](https://docs.rs/trait.Append.html)
- An appender that can process log records.
- [Diagnostic](https://docs.rs/trait.Diagnostic.html)
- A Mapped Diagnostic Context (MDC) that provides diagnostic key-values.
- [Filter](https://docs.rs/trait.Filter.html)
- A filter that can be applied to log records.
- [Layout](https://docs.rs/trait.Layout.html)
- A layout for formatting log records.

# fern - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fern/*/fern/

## Expand description

Efficient, configurable logging in Rust.

[§](https://docs.rs#fern-044-05-06-security-warning---colored-feature--global-allocator)fern 0.4.4, 0.5.*, 0.6.* security warning - `colored` feature + global allocator

One of our downstream dependencies, [atty](https://docs.rs/atty/), through
[colored](https://docs.rs/colored/), has an unsoundness issue:
[https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2021-0145.html](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2021-0145.html).

This shows up in one situation: if you’re using `colored` 0.1.0 (the crate, or our
feature), and a custom global allocator.

Upgrade to `fern` 0.7.0, and `colored` 0.2.0 if you depend on it directly, to fix this issue.

[§](https://docs.rs#depending-on-fern)Depending on fern

Ensure you require both fern and log in your project’s `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
log = "0.4"
fern = "0.7"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-setup)Example setup

With fern, all logger configuration is done via builder-like methods on
instances of the [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/struct.Dispatch.html) structure.

Here’s an example logger which formats messages, and sends everything Debug and above to both stdout and an output.log file:

```
use log::{debug, error, info, trace, warn};
use std::time::SystemTime;
fn setup_logger() -> Result<(), fern::InitError> {
    fern::Dispatch::new()
        .format(|out, message, record| {
            out.finish(format_args!(
                "[{} {} {}] {}",
                humantime::format_rfc3339_seconds(SystemTime::now()),
                record.level(),
                record.target(),
                message
            ))
        })
        .level(log::LevelFilter::Debug)
        .chain(std::io::stdout())
        .chain(fern::log_file("output.log")?)
        .apply()?;
    Ok(())
}
fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    setup_logger()?;
    info!("Hello, world!");
    warn!("Warning!");
    debug!("Now exiting.");
    Ok(())
}
```
Let’s unwrap this:

`fern::Dispatch::new()`[ Dispatch::new](https://docs.rs/struct.Dispatch.html#method.new) creates an empty configuration.

```
.format(|out, message, record| {
    out.finish(format_args!(
        "..."
    ))
})
```
This incantation sets the `Dispatch` format! The closure taking in
`out, message, record` will be called once for each message going through
the dispatch, and the formatted log message will be used for any downstream
consumers.

Do any work you want in this closure, and then call `out.finish` at the end.
The callback-style result passing with `out.finish(format_args!())` lets us
format without any intermediate string allocation.

[ format_args!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.format_args.html) has the same format as

[, just returning a not-yet-written result we can use internally.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/macro.println.html)

`println!``std::time::SystemTime::now()`[ std::time::SystemTime::now](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/time/struct.SystemTime.html#method.now) retrieves the current time.

```
humantime::format_rfc3339_seconds(
    // ...
)
```
[ humantime::format_rfc3339_seconds](https://docs.rs/humantime/2/humantime/fn.format_rfc3339_seconds.html) formats the current time into an
RFC3339 timestamp, with second-precision.

RFC3339 looks like `2018-02-14T00:28:07Z`, always using UTC, ignoring system
timezone.

`humantime` is a nice light dependency, but only offers this one format.
For more custom time formatting, I recommend
[ jiff](https://docs.rs/jiff/).

Now, back to the [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/struct.Dispatch.html) methods:

`.level(log::LevelFilter::Debug)`Sets the minimum logging level for all modules, if not overwritten with
[ Dispatch::level_for](https://docs.rs/struct.Dispatch.html#method.level_for), to

[.](https://docs.rs/log/0.3.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.Level.html#variant.Debug)

`Level::Debug``.chain(std::io::stdout())`Adds a child to the logger. With this, all messages which pass the filters will be sent to stdout.

[ Dispatch::chain](https://docs.rs/struct.Dispatch.html#method.chain) accepts

[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/stdio/struct.Stdout.html)

`Stdout`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/stdio/struct.Stderr.html)

`Stderr`[and other](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html)

`File`[instances.](https://docs.rs/struct.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch``.chain(fern::log_file("output.log")?)`Adds a second child sending messages to the file “output.log”.

See [ log_file](https://docs.rs/fn.log_file.html).

```
// ...
.apply()
```
Consumes the configuration and instantiates it as the current runtime global logger.

This will fail if and only if `.apply()` or equivalent form another crate
has already been used this runtime.

Since the binary crate is the only one ever setting up logging, and it’s
usually done near the start of `main`, the [ Dispatch::apply](https://docs.rs/struct.Dispatch.html#method.apply) result can be
reasonably unwrapped: it’s a bug if any crate is calling this method more
than once.

The final output will look like:

```
[2023-03-18T20:12:50Z INFO cmd_program] Hello, world!
[2023-03-18T20:12:50Z WARN cmd_program] Warning!
[2023-03-18T20:12:50Z DEBUG cmd_program] Now exiting.
```
[§](https://docs.rs#logging)Logging

Once the logger has been set, it will pick up all logging calls from your crate and all libraries you depend on.

```
fern::Dispatch::new()
    // ...
    .apply()?;
trace!("Trace message");
debug!("Debug message");
info!("Info message");
warn!("Warning message");
error!("Error message");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#more)More

The [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/struct.Dispatch.html) documentation has example usages of each method, and the

[full example program](https://github.com/daboross/fern/tree/fern-0.7.0/examples/cmd-program.rs)might be useful for using fern in a larger application context.

See the [colors](https://docs.rs/colors/index.html) module for examples using ANSI terminal coloring.

See the [syslog](https://docs.rs/syslog/index.html) module for examples outputting to the unix syslog, or the
[syslog full example program](https://github.com/daboross/fern/tree/fern-0.7.0/examples/syslog.rs) for a more realistic sample.

See the [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html) module for information on getting logging-within-logging
working correctly.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [colors](https://docs.rs/colors/index.html)
- Support for ANSI terminal colors via the colored crate.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)
- Fern supports logging most things by default, except for one kind of struct: structs which make log
calls to the global logger from within their `Display`or`Debug`implementations.
- [syslog](https://docs.rs/syslog/index.html)
- Example usage of `fern`with the`syslog`crate.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Date](https://docs.rs/struct.DateBased.html)- Based
- This is used to generate log file suffixed based on date, hour, and minute.
- [Dispatch](https://docs.rs/struct.Dispatch.html)
- The base dispatch logger.
- [Format](https://docs.rs/struct.FormatCallback.html)- Callback
- Callback struct for use within a formatter closure
- [Output](https://docs.rs/struct.Output.html)
- Configuration for a logger output.
- [Panic](https://docs.rs/struct.Panic.html)
- Logger which will panic whenever anything is logged. The panic will be exactly the message of the log.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Init](https://docs.rs/enum.InitError.html)- Error
- Convenience error combining possible errors which could occur while initializing logging.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [log_](https://docs.rs/fn.log_file.html)- file
- Convenience method for opening a log file with common options.
- [log_](https://docs.rs/fn.log_reopen.html)- reopen
- Convenience method for opening a re-openable log file with common options.
- [log_](https://docs.rs/fn.log_reopen1.html)- reopen1
- Convenience method for opening a re-openable log file with common options.

# spdlog - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/spdlog-rs/*/spdlog/

## Expand description

Fast, highly configurable Rust logging crate.

It is inspired by the C++ logging library [spdlog](https://github.com/gabime/spdlog), and we share most of the
same concepts. So if you are already familiar with C++ `spdlog`, you should
be able to get started with this crate quite easily. Of course, there are
some differences, you can see [Significant differences from C++
spdlog](https://docs.rs#significant-differences-from-c-spdlog) below.

[§](https://docs.rs#table-of-contents)Table of contents

[§](https://docs.rs#overview-of-features)Overview of features

- [Configured via environment variable](https://docs.rs/fn.init_env_level.html)
- [Compile-time and runtime pattern formatter](https://docs.rs/formatter/index.html#compile-time-and-runtime-pattern-formatter)
- [Asynchronous support](https://docs.rs/sink/struct.AsyncPoolSink.html)
- [Structured logging](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html)
- [Compatible with log crate](https://docs.rs/struct.LogCrateProxy.html)
- [Capturing logs in tests](https://docs.rs/sink/struct.StdStreamSinkBuilder.html#method.via_print_macro)

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

Add this to `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
spdlog-rs = "0.5"
```
`spdlog-rs` is highly configurable, and also works out-of-the-box for
lightweight projects. By default, logs will be output to `stdout` and
`stderr`.

```
use spdlog::prelude::*;
// Non-severe logs (trace, debug) are ignored by default.
// If you wish to enable all logs, call
spdlog::default_logger().set_level_filter(spdlog::LevelFilter::All);
info!("hello, world!");
error!("oops!");
debug!("3 + 2 = {}", 5);
```
Output:

[2022-11-02 09:23:12.263] [info] hello, world! [2022-11-02 09:23:12.263] [error] oops! [2022-11-02 09:23:12.263] [debug] 3 + 2 = 5

The basic use is through these logging macros: [ trace!](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html)

`error!`[, where](https://docs.rs/macro.critical.html)

`critical!``critical!`
represents the most severe logs and `trace!` the most verbose. Each of these
macros accept format strings similarly to [. All log macros and common types are already under](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/macro.println.html)

`println!`[module.](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude`[§](https://docs.rs#sink)Sink

Many real programs want more than just displaying logs to the terminal.

[ Sink](https://docs.rs/sink/trait.Sink.html)s are the objects that actually write logs to their targets. If you
want logs to be written to files as well,

[is what you need.](https://docs.rs/sink/struct.FileSink.html)

`FileSink````
use spdlog::{prelude::*, sink::FileSink};
let path = "path/to/somewhere.log";
let new_logger = spdlog::default_logger().fork_with(|new| {
    let file_sink = FileSink::builder().path(path).build_arc()?;
    new.sinks_mut().push(file_sink);
    Ok(())
})?;
spdlog::set_default_logger(new_logger);
info!("from now on, logs will be written to both stdout/stderr and the file");
```
Take a look at [ sink](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html) module for more interesting sinks, such as

[that automatically rotates files by time point or file size, and](https://docs.rs/sink/struct.RotatingFileSink.html)

`RotatingFileSink`[that outputs logs asynchronously.](https://docs.rs/sink/struct.AsyncPoolSink.html)

`AsyncPoolSink`[§](https://docs.rs#logger)Logger

A complex program may consist of many separated components.

[ Logger](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html) manages, controls and manipulates multiple sinks within it. In
addition to having the global

[, more loggers are allowed to be configured, stored and used independently.](https://docs.rs/fn.default_logger.html)

`default_logger`Logging macros provide an optional parameter `logger`. If it is specified,
logs will be processed by the specified logger instead of the global default
logger.

And benefiting from the fact that a logger uses `Arc` to store sinks, a sink
can be set and used by more than one logger, and you can combine them as you
like.

```
use spdlog::prelude::*;
struct AppDatabase {
    logger: Logger,
    // Database info...
}
impl AppDatabase {
    fn new() -> Result<Self> {
        let logger = Logger::builder()
            .name("database")
            // .sink( ... )
            // .sink( ... )
            // .level_filter( ... )
            // ...
            .build()?;
        Ok(Self { logger, /* Database info... */ })
    }
    fn query<T>(&self) -> T {
        let data = /* Query from the database */
        trace!(logger: self.logger, "queried data {}", data);
        data
    }
}
struct AppNetwork { /* ... */ }
struct AppAuth { /* ... */ }
struct AppBlahBlah { /* ... */ }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#learn-more)Learn more

Directory [./examples](https://github.com/SpriteOvO/spdlog-rs/tree/main/spdlog/examples) contains more advanced usage examples. You can learn
them along with their documentation.

If you have any trouble while using this crate, please don’t hesitate to
[open a discussion](https://github.com/SpriteOvO/spdlog-rs/discussions/new) for help. For feature requests or bug reports, please
[open an issue](https://github.com/SpriteOvO/spdlog-rs/issues/new/choose).

[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-filters)Compile-time filters

Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time via Cargo features. Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the resulting binary. This level is configured separately for release and debug builds. The features are:

- `level-off`
- `level-critical`
- `level-error`
- `level-warn`
- `level-info`
- `level-debug`
- `level-trace`
- `release-level-off`
- `release-level-critical`
- `release-level-error`
- `release-level-warn`
- `release-level-info`
- `release-level-debug`
- `release-level-trace`

These features control the value of the `STATIC_LEVEL_FILTER` constant. The
logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no
levels are disabled.

For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace,
debug, and info level logs in release builds with
`features = ["level-debug", "release-level-warn"]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate feature flags

The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters.
They are configured in your `Cargo.toml`.

-
`source-location`allows recording the source location of each log. When it is enabled, the source location will be present in`Record``Formatter`
-
`flexible-string`improves the performance of formatting records, however it contains unsafe code. For more details, see the documentation of`StringBuf`
-
`log`enables the compatibility with[log crate](https://crates.io/crates/log).
-
`native`enables platform-specific components, such as`sink::WinDebugSink``sink::JournaldSink`
-
`runtime-pattern`enables the ability to build patterns with runtime template string. See`RuntimePattern`
-
`serde_json`enables`formatter::JsonFormatter`
-
`std-stream-captured`changes the default behavior of`StdStreamSink``StdStreamSinkBuilder::via_print_macro`

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-rust-versions)Supported Rust versions

The current minimum supported Rust version is 1.71.

`spdlog-rs` is built against the latest Rust stable release, it is not
guaranteed to build on Rust versions earlier than the minimum supported
version.

`spdlog-rs` follows the compiler support policy that the latest stable
version and the 3 most recent minor versions before that are always
supported. For example, if the current latest Rust stable version is 1.61,
the minimum supported version will not be increased past 1.58. Increasing
the minimum supported version is not considered a semver breaking change as
long as it complies with this policy.

[§](https://docs.rs#significant-differences-from-c-spdlog)Significant differences from C++ spdlog

The significant differences between `spdlog-rs` and C++ `spdlog` 1:

-
`spdlog-rs`does not have`registry`[2](https://docs.rs#fn2)
-
`spdlog-rs`does not have`backtrace`[2](https://docs.rs#fn2)
-
In `spdlog-rs`,`LevelFilter`
-
In `spdlog-rs`, there is no “_st” sinks, all sinks are “_mt”.
-
`daily_file_sink`and`hourly_file_sink`in C++`spdlog`are merged into`RotatingFileSink``spdlog-rs`. They correspond to rotation policies`RotationPolicy::Daily``RotationPolicy::Hourly`
-
`async_logger`in C++`spdlog`is`AsyncPoolSink``spdlog-rs`. This allows it to be used with synchronous sinks.
-
Some sinks in C++ `spdlog`are not yet implemented in`spdlog-rs`. (Yes, PRs are welcome)
-
…

# syslog - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syslog/*/syslog/

## Expand description

Syslog

This crate provides facilities to send log messages via syslog. It supports Unix sockets for local syslog, UDP and TCP for remote servers.

Messages can be passed directly without modification, or in RFC 3164 or RFC 5424 format

The code is available on [Github](https://github.com/Geal/rust-syslog)

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use syslog::{Facility, Formatter3164};
let formatter = Formatter3164 {
    facility: Facility::LOG_USER,
    hostname: None,
    process: "myprogram".into(),
    pid: 0,
};
match syslog::unix(formatter) {
    Err(e) => println!("impossible to connect to syslog: {:?}", e),
    Ok(mut writer) => {
        writer.err("hello world").expect("could not write error message");
    }
}
```
It can be used directly with the log crate as follows:

```
extern crate log;
use syslog::{Facility, Formatter3164, BasicLogger};
use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter, info};
let formatter = Formatter3164 {
    facility: Facility::LOG_USER,
    hostname: None,
    process: "myprogram".into(),
    pid: 0,
};
let logger = match syslog::unix(formatter) {
    Err(e) => { println!("impossible to connect to syslog: {:?}", e); return; },
    Ok(logger) => logger,
};
log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(BasicLogger::new(logger)))
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info));
info!("hello world");
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Basic](https://docs.rs/struct.BasicLogger.html)- Logger
- [Formatter3164](https://docs.rs/struct.Formatter3164.html)
- [Formatter5424](https://docs.rs/struct.Formatter5424.html)
- [Logger](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html)
- Main logging structure

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html)
- Initializes logging subsystem for log crate
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_tcp.html)- tcp
- TCP Logger init function compatible with log crate
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_udp.html)- udp
- UDP Logger init function compatible with log crate
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_unix.html)- unix
- Unix socket Logger init function compatible with log crate
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_unix_custom.html)- unix_ - custom
- Unix socket Logger init function compatible with log crate and user provided socket path
- [tcp](https://docs.rs/fn.tcp.html)
- returns a TCP logger connecting `local`and`server`
- [udp](https://docs.rs/fn.udp.html)
- returns a UDP logger connecting `local`and`server`
- [unix](https://docs.rs/fn.unix.html)
- Returns a Logger using unix socket to target local syslog ( using /dev/log or /var/run/syslog)
- [unix_](https://docs.rs/fn.unix_custom.html)- custom
- Returns a Logger using unix socket to target local syslog at user provided path

# slog_stdlog - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/slog-stdlog/*/slog_stdlog/

## Expand description

`log` crate adapter for slog-rs

This crate provides two way compatibility with Rust standard `log` crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#log---slog)`log` -> `slog`

After calling `init()` `slog-stdlog` will take a role of `log` crate
back-end, forwarding all the `log` logging to `slog_scope::logger()`.
In other words, any `log` crate logging statement will behave like it was `slog`
logging statement executed with logger returned by `slog_scope::logger()`.

See documentation of `slog-scope` for more information about logging scopes.

See [ init documentation](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html) for an example.

[§](https://docs.rs#slog---log)`slog` -> `log`

`StdLog` is `slog::Drain` that will pass all `Record`s passing through it to
`log` crate just like they were crated with `log` crate logging macros in
the first place.

[§](https://docs.rs#slog-scope)`slog-scope`

Since `log` does not have any form of context, and does not support `Logger`
`slog-stdlog` relies on “logging scopes” to establish it.

You must set up logging context for `log` -> `slog` via `slog_scope::scope`
or `slog_scope::set_global_logger`. Setting a global logger upfront via
`slog_scope::set_global_logger` is highly recommended.

Note: Since `slog-stdlog` v2, unlike previous releases, `slog-stdlog` uses
logging scopes provided by `slog-scope` crate instead of it’s own.

Refer to `slog-scope` crate documentation for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

Be careful when using both methods at the same time, as a loop can be easily
created: `log` -> `slog` -> `log` -> …

[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-log-level-filtering)Compile-time log level filtering

For filtering `debug!` and other `log` statements at compile-time, configure
the features on the `log` crate in your `Cargo.toml`:

`log = { version = "*", features = ["max_level_trace", "release_max_level_warn"] }`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [StdLog](https://docs.rs/struct.StdLog.html)
- Drain logging `Record`s into`log`crate

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html)
- Register `slog-stdlog`as`log`backend.
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_with_level.html)- with_ - level
- Register `slog-stdlog`as`log`backend. Pass a log::Level to do the log filter explicitly.

# systemd_journal_logger - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/systemd-journal-logger/*/systemd_journal_logger/

## Expand description

A pure Rust [log](https://docs.rs/log) logger for the [systemd journal](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/journalctl.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Create a [ JournalLog](https://docs.rs/struct.JournalLog.html) with

[and then use](https://docs.rs/struct.JournalLog.html#method.new)

`JournalLog::new`[to setup journal logging. Then configure the logging level and now you can use the standard macros from the](https://docs.rs/struct.JournalLog.html#method.install)

`JournalLog::install`[crate to send log messages to the systemd journal:](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.26/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/index.html)

`log````
use log::{info, warn, error, LevelFilter};
use systemd_journal_logger::JournalLog;
JournalLog::new().unwrap().install().unwrap();
log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info);
info!("hello log");
warn!("warning");
error!("oops");
```
See [ JournalLog](https://docs.rs/struct.JournalLog.html) for details about the logging format.

[§](https://docs.rs#journal-connections)Journal connections

In a service you can use [ connected_to_journal](https://docs.rs/fn.connected_to_journal.html) to check whether
the standard output or error stream of the current process is directly
connected to the systemd journal (the default for services started by
systemd) and fall back to logging to standard error if that’s not the
case.  Take a look at the

[systemd_service.rs](https://codeberg.org/swsnr/systemd-journal-logger.rs/src/branch/main/examples/systemd_service.rs)example for details.

```
use log::{info, warn, error, LevelFilter};
use systemd_journal_logger::JournalLog;
JournalLog::new()
    .unwrap()
    .with_extra_fields(vec![("VERSION", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))])
    .with_syslog_identifier("foo".to_string())
    .install().unwrap();
log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info);
info!("this message has an extra VERSION field in the journal");
```
You can display these extra fields with `journalctl --output=verbose` and extract them with any of the structured
output formats of `journalctl`, e.g. `journalctl --output=json`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Journal](https://docs.rs/struct.JournalLog.html)- Log
- A systemd journal logger.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [connected_](https://docs.rs/fn.connected_to_journal.html)- to_ - journal
- Whether the current process is directly connected to the systemd journal.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_exe_identifier.html)- exe_ - identifier
- Create a syslog identifier from the current executable.

# android_log - Rust

## Expand description

A logger which writes to the Android logging subsystem. It must be compiled
with the Android NDK in order to link to `liblog`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
#[macro_use] extern crate log;
extern crate android_log;
fn main() {
    android_log::init("MyApp").unwrap();
    trace!("Initialized Rust");
    debug!("Address is {:p}", main as *const ());
    info!("Did you know? {} = {}", "1 + 1", 2);
    warn!("Don't log sensitive information!");
    error!("Nothing more to say");
}
```
```
$ logcat
12-25 12:00:00.000  1234  1234 V MyApp: Initialized Rust
12-25 12:00:00.000  1234  1234 D MyApp: Address is 0xdeadbeef
12-25 12:00:00.000  1234  1234 I MyApp: Did you know? 1 + 1 = 2
12-25 12:00:00.000  1234  1234 W MyApp: Don't log sensitive information!
12-25 12:00:00.000  1234  1234 E MyApp: Nothing more to say
```

# win_dbg_logger - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/win_dbg_logger/*/win_dbg_logger/

## Expand description

A logger for use with Windows debuggers.

Windows allows applications to output a string directly to debuggers. This is very useful in situations where other forms of logging are not available. For example, stderr is not available for GUI apps.

Windows provides the `OutputDebugString` entry point, which allows apps to
print a debug string. Internally, `OutputDebugString` is implemented by
raising an SEH exception, which the debugger catches and handles.

Raising an exception has a significant cost, when run under a debugger, because the debugger halts all threads in the target process. So you should avoid using this logger for high rates of output, because doing so will slow down your app.

Like many Windows entry points, `OutputDebugString` is actually two entry
points: `OutputDebugStringA` (multi-byte encodings) and
`OutputDebugStringW` (UTF-16). In most cases, the `*A` version is implemented
using a “thunk” which converts its arguments to UTF-16 and then calls the `*W`
version. However, `OutputDebugStringA` is one of the few entry points where
the opposite is true.

This crate can be compiled and used on non-Windows platforms, but it does nothing. This is intended to minimize the impact on code that takes a dependency on this crate.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Debugger](https://docs.rs/struct.DebuggerLogger.html)- Logger
- This implements `log::Log`, and so can be used as a logging provider. It forwards log messages to the Windows`OutputDebugString`API.

## Statics[§](https://docs.rs#statics)

- [DEBUGGER_](https://docs.rs/static.DEBUGGER_LOGGER.html)- LOGGER
- This is a static instance of `DebuggerLogger`. Since`DebuggerLogger`contains no state, this can be directly registered using`log::set_logger`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html)
- Sets the `DebuggerLogger`as the currently-active logger.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_debugger_present.html)- debugger_ - present
- Checks whether a debugger is attached to the current process.
- [output_](https://docs.rs/fn.output_debug_string.html)- debug_ - string
- Calls the `OutputDebugString`API to log a string.
- [rust_](https://docs.rs/fn.rust_win_dbg_logger_init_debug.html)- win_ - dbg_ - logger_ - init_ - debug
- This can be called from C/C++ code to register the debug logger.
- [rust_](https://docs.rs/fn.rust_win_dbg_logger_init_error.html)- win_ - dbg_ - logger_ - init_ - error
- This can be called from C/C++ code to register the debug logger.
- [rust_](https://docs.rs/fn.rust_win_dbg_logger_init_info.html)- win_ - dbg_ - logger_ - init_ - info
- This can be called from C/C++ code to register the debug logger.
- [rust_](https://docs.rs/fn.rust_win_dbg_logger_init_trace.html)- win_ - dbg_ - logger_ - init_ - trace
- This can be called from C/C++ code to register the debug logger.
- [rust_](https://docs.rs/fn.rust_win_dbg_logger_init_warn.html)- win_ - dbg_ - logger_ - init_ - warn
- This can be called from C/C++ code to register the debug logger.

# log_to_defmt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log-to-defmt/*/log_to_defmt/

## Expand description

This is a logging adapter that acts as an implementation of the [log crate](https://crates.io/crates/log) and hands the
rendered messages off to the [defmt crate](https://crates.io/crates/defmt).

Using this is generally not recommended: Once the log infrastructure is pulled into a project, Rust’s string formatting is brought in, avoiding which is a big part of the point of defmt.

However, this can be useful during development, when debugging a particular library (that optionally produces messages through log) on a platform for which a defmt output has already been established.

[§](https://docs.rs#maturity)Maturity

The current implementation of this takes a huge amount of shortcuts: not only does it not convert log levels, it also hardwires some to the most verbose level, discards lots of information that would otherwise be available, and uses a fixed size buffer.

Future iterations of this crate are expected to address these on demand; for example, this
could gain a build time configuration mechanism for the maximum expected length, or an `alloc`
feature that renders the log messages to a `Vec` instead of a `heapless::Vec` before handing
them off to defmt as a slice.

The crate will likely introduce such features (altering its behavior) without declaring breaking changes; users are advised to configure their error levels to match which messages they expect to see.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [setup](https://docs.rs/fn.setup.html)
- Set up log output to be forwarded to defmt

---

# logcontrol_log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/logcontrol-log/*/logcontrol_log/

## Expand description

A [ LogControl1](https://docs.rs/logcontrol/1.0.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/logcontrol/trait.LogControl1.html) implementation for

[.](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/index.html)

`log`[ LogController](https://docs.rs/struct.LogController.html) provides a

[implementation on top of](https://docs.rs/logcontrol/1.0.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/logcontrol/trait.LogControl1.html)

`LogControl1`[which uses the](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/index.html)

`log`[crate to dynamically switch loggers and levels depending on the target and level selected over the log control interface.](https://docs.rs/log-reload/0.1.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log_reload/index.html)

`log_reload`It uses a [ LogFactory](https://docs.rs/trait.LogFactory.html) implementation to create the actual

[instances each time the log target is changed. This crates provides](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/trait.Log.html)

`Log`*no*default implementation of this trait; users have to provide an implementation on their own. This avoids a dependency on any specific log implementation for the

`console` target.For the `journal` target this crate uses the [ systemd_journal_logger](https://docs.rs/systemd-journal-logger/2.2.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/systemd_journal_logger/index.html) crate.

See [ LogController::install_auto](https://docs.rs/struct.LogController.html#method.install_auto) for the recommended entry point to this crate.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [logcontrol](https://docs.rs/logcontrol/1.0.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/logcontrol/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A `LogControl1``log`

# console_log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/console_log/*/console_log/

## Expand description

A logger that logs to the browser’s console.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use log::Level;
use log::info;
fn main() {
    console_log::init_with_level(Level::Debug);
    info!("It works!");
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#log-levels)Log Levels

Rust’s log levels map to the browser’s console log in the following way.

| Rust | Web Console |
|---|---|
| `trace!()` | `console.debug()` |
| `debug!()` | `console.log()` |
| `info!()` | `console.info()` |
| `warn!()` | `console.warn()` |
| `error!()` | `console.error()` |

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-fancy)Getting Fancy

The feature set provided by this crate is intentionally very basic. If you need more flexible
formatting of log messages (timestamps, file and line info, etc.) this crate can be used with
the [ fern](https://docs.rs/fern) logger via the

[function.](https://docs.rs/fn.log.html)

`console_log::log`[§](https://docs.rs#colors)Colors

The `"color"` feature adds styling to the log messages.

`Cargo.toml`

`console_log = { version = "0.2", features = ["color"] }`The styled log messages will be rendered as follows:

[§](https://docs.rs#code-size)Code Size

[Twiggy](https://github.com/rustwasm/twiggy) reports this library adding about 180Kb to the size of a minimal wasm binary in a
debug build. If you want to avoid this, mark the library as optional and conditionally
initialize it in your code for non-release builds.

`Cargo.toml`

```
[dependencies]
cfg-if = "0.1"
log = "0.4"
console_log = { version = "0.2", optional = true }
[features]
default = ["console_log"]
```
`lib.rs`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;
use cfg_if::cfg_if;
cfg_if! {
    if #[cfg(feature = "console_log")] {
        fn init_log() {
            use log::Level;
            console_log::init_with_level(Level::Trace).expect("error initializing log");
        }
    } else {
        fn init_log() {}
    }
}
#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn main() {
    init_log();
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

The file and line number information associated with the log messages reports locations from
the shims generated by `wasm-bindgen`, not the location of the logger call.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html)
- Initializes the global logger with `max_log_level`set to`Level::Info`(a sensible default).
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_with_level.html)- with_ - level
- Initializes the global logger setting `max_log_level`to the given value.
- [log](https://docs.rs/fn.log.html)
- Print a `log::Record`to the browser’s console at the appropriate level.

# log_err - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log_err/*/log_err/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#log_err)Log_Err

A small extension to the [log](https://crates.io/crates/log) crate, which provides two methods for `core::result::Result<T, E>` and `core::option::Option<T>`

`log_except` and `log_unwrap`, which invoke the `log::error!` macro (in case of `Result::Err`) in *addition* to unwrapping/expecting the `Result`.

Shorthand for:

Example:

```
# Error will be logged with the error! macro
[ERROR] Error creating file: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }
# Main program panic'ing with same message
thread 'main' panicked at 'Error creating file: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }', test.rs:4:48
```

---

# log_reload - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log-reload/*/log_reload/

## Expand description

A [ log::Log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/trait.Log.html) implementation which dynamically reloads inner loggers.

[ ReloadLog](https://docs.rs/struct.ReloadLog.html) wraps an inner logger and provides a

[to dynamically replace or modify the inner logger.](https://docs.rs/struct.ReloadHandle.html)

`ReloadHandle`This allows programs to dynamically change the log level or log target at runtime.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Level](https://docs.rs/struct.LevelFilter.html)- Filter
- Filter an underlying logger by a given max level.
- [Reload](https://docs.rs/struct.ReloadHandle.html)- Handle
- A handle to reload a logger inside a `ReloadLog`
- [Reload](https://docs.rs/struct.ReloadLog.html)- Log
- A logger which can dynamically reload an inner logger.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Reload](https://docs.rs/enum.ReloadError.html)- Error
- An error which occurred while reloading the logger.

# Log in log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/^0.4/trait.Log.html

`pub trait Log: `[Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html) + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) {
    // Required methods
    fn [enabled](https://docs.rs#tymethod.enabled)(&self, metadata: &[Metadata](https://docs.rs/struct.Metadata.html)<'_>) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html);
[log](https://docs.rs#tymethod.log)(&self, record: &[Record](https://docs.rs/struct.Record.html)<'_>);
[flush](https://docs.rs#tymethod.flush)(&self);
}## Expand description

A trait encapsulating the operations required of a logger.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Determines if a log message with the specified metadata would be logged.

This is used by the `log_enabled!` macro to allow callers to avoid
expensive computation of log message arguments if the message would be
discarded anyway.

[§](https://docs.rs#for-implementors)For implementors

This method isn’t called automatically by the `log!` macros.
It’s up to an implementation of the `Log` trait to call `enabled` in its own
`log` method implementation to guarantee that filtering is applied.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Level in log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/^0.4/enum.Level.html

```
#[repr(usize)]pub enum Level {
    Error = 1,
    Warn = 2,
    Info = 3,
    Debug = 4,
    Trace = 5,
}
```
## Expand description

An enum representing the available verbosity levels of the logger.

Typical usage includes: checking if a certain `Level` is enabled with
[ log_enabled!](https://docs.rs/macro.log_enabled.html), specifying the

`Level` of
[, and comparing a](https://docs.rs/macro.log.html)

`log!``Level` directly to a
[.](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`LevelFilter`## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Error)

### Error = 1

The “error” level.

Designates very serious errors.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Warn)

### Warn = 2

The “warn” level.

Designates hazardous situations.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Info)

### Info = 3

The “info” level.

Designates useful information.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Debug)

### Debug = 4

The “debug” level.

Designates lower priority information.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Trace)

### Trace = 5

The “trace” level.

Designates very low priority, often extremely verbose, information.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Returns the string representation of the `Level`.

This returns the same string as the `fmt::Display` implementation.

Iterate through all supported logging levels.

The order of iteration is from more severe to less severe log messages.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::Level;
let mut levels = Level::iter();
assert_eq!(Some(Level::Error), levels.next());
assert_eq!(Some(Level::Trace), levels.last());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/log/lib.rs.html#599-602)#### pub fn [increment_severity](https://docs.rs#method.increment_severity)(&self) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/log/lib.rs.html#599-602)

#### pub fn [increment_severity](https://docs.rs#method.increment_severity)(&self) -> Self

Get the next-highest `Level` from this one.

If the current `Level` is at the highest level, the returned `Level` will be the same as the
current one.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use log::Level;
let level = Level::Info;
assert_eq!(Level::Debug, level.increment_severity());
assert_eq!(Level::Trace, level.increment_severity().increment_severity());
assert_eq!(Level::Trace, level.increment_severity().increment_severity().increment_severity()); // max level
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/log/lib.rs.html#620-623)#### pub fn [decrement_severity](https://docs.rs#method.decrement_severity)(&self) -> Self

#### pub fn [decrement_severity](https://docs.rs#method.decrement_severity)(&self) -> Self

Get the next-lowest `Level` from this one.

If the current `Level` is at the lowest level, the returned `Level` will be the same as the
current one.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

# set_logger in log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/^0.4/fn.set_logger.html

`pub fn set_logger(logger: &'static dyn `[Log](https://docs.rs/trait.Log.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [SetLoggerError](https://docs.rs/struct.SetLoggerError.html)>## Expand description

Sets the global logger to a `&'static Log`.

This function may only be called once in the lifetime of a program. Any log
events that occur before the call to `set_logger` completes will be ignored.

This function does not typically need to be called manually. Logger implementations should provide an initialization method that installs the logger internally.

[§](https://docs.rs#availability)Availability

This method is available even when the `std` feature is disabled. However,
it is currently unavailable on `thumbv6` targets, which lack support for
some atomic operations which are used by this function. Even on those
targets, [ set_logger_racy](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger_racy.html) will be available.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

An error is returned if a logger has already been set.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::{error, info, warn, Record, Level, Metadata, LevelFilter};
static MY_LOGGER: MyLogger = MyLogger;
struct MyLogger;
impl log::Log for MyLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= Level::Info
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
        if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
        }
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
log::set_logger(&MY_LOGGER).unwrap();
log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info);
info!("hello log");
warn!("warning");
error!("oops");
```

---

# set_max_level in log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/^0.4/fn.set_max_level.html

`pub fn set_max_level(level: `[LevelFilter](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html))## Expand description

Sets the global maximum log level.

Generally, this should only be called by the active logging implementation.

Note that `Trace` is the maximum level, because it provides the maximum amount of detail in the emitted logs.

# LevelFilter in log - Rust

#[repr(usize)]pub enum LevelFilter {
    Off = 0,
    Error = 1,
    Warn = 2,
    Info = 3,
    Debug = 4,
    Trace = 5,

## Expand description

An enum representing the available verbosity level filters of the logger.

A `LevelFilter` may be compared directly to a [ Level](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html). Use this type
to get and set the maximum log level with

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.max_level.html)

### Warn = 2
